ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9001.q: A domestic assembler sells $420,000 of new equipment, using $150,000 of imported parts and $90,000 of current domestic components. A clerk adds all three values as domestic GDP. What correction reconciles final spending with domestic value added?
options: $270,000 total domestic GDP, including $180,000 at assembly
$420,000 total domestic GDP, including $330,000 at assembly
$510,000 total domestic GDP, including $420,000 at assembly
$180,000 total domestic GDP, excluding the domestic component makers

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9001.reason: C/D: replace two-country recognition with imported-input and value-added reconciliation.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9003.q: A workshop sells $560 of new furniture after buying $140 of domestic lumber. Its wage bill is $250 and rent plus interest is $90. With no other costs or taxes, which value-added and profit account is consistent?
options: $420 value added, including $80 profit
$560 value added, including $220 profit
$280 value added, including $80 profit
$420 value added, including $420 profit
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9003.feedback: Value added is final output less intermediate lumber: 560 - 140 = 420. Of that, wages and rent/interest absorb 340, leaving profit of 80. Subtracting wages when computing value added would remove income generated by production.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9003.reason: C/D: link intermediate goods, value added and residual production income.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9009.q: A renovation business bills households $96,000, including $24,000 of imported fixtures. It also brokers an old building for a $6,000 fee; the building sells for $310,000. Ignoring other inputs, what current domestic production and counting rule follow?
options: $78,000; count domestic renovation value and the new brokerage service
$388,000; the old building becomes current output when sold
$102,000; imported fixtures count because households bought them
$72,000; services attached to used assets must also be excluded
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9009.feedback: Domestic renovation value is 96,000 - 24,000 = 72,000. The current brokerage service adds 6,000, while the old building itself is not new output. Total current domestic production is 78,000.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9009.reason: C/D: distinguish used asset from a new service and remove imported inputs.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9010.q: A production audit reports $74 million of final sales and $6 million of new inventories. Domestic production income is $51 million in wages, $9 million in rent and interest, and unreported profit. With no imports, taxes or depreciation adjustments, which result closes both accounts?
options: $80 million GDP and $20 million profit
$74 million GDP and $14 million profit
$86 million GDP and $26 million profit
$60 million GDP and $20 million profit

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9010.reason: C/D: infer missing income from sales plus unsold production.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9011.q: A used machine changes hands for $40,000 through a broker charging $2,000. A new domestic machine worth $28,000 is produced but remains unsold. An analyst counts only the $40,000 resale as this year’s GDP. What is the corrected contribution?
options: $30,000: brokerage service plus inventory investment
$42,000: resale plus brokerage service
$70,000: every transaction and unsold machine
$2,000: unsold output cannot count until purchased

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9011.reason: B/C: replace repeated used-good definition with timing and current-service accounting.

ECON-NL-ELITE-303.q: A mill sells $180 of flour made from $70 of current domestic grain. A baker uses all the flour in $310 of bread sold to households. What are the baker’s value added and GDP across the full domestic chain?
options: $130 at the bakery; $310 across the chain
$240 at the bakery; $560 across the chain
$310 at the bakery; $310 across the chain
$130 at the bakery; $490 across the chain
ECON-NL-ELITE-303.feedback: The baker adds 310 - 180 = 130. Summing domestic value added gives 70 + (180 - 70) + 130 = 310, equal to the final sale. Intermediate sales cannot be added again.
ECON-NL-ELITE-303.reason: D: make value-added arithmetic support the full-chain interpretation.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9000.q: An economy reports C = 46, G = 13, exports = 9, imports = 11, and GDP = 72, all in billions. A separate inventory report records 4 billion of new unsold output. What investment total reconciles the accounts, and how should the inventory figure be treated?
options: I = 15; the 4 of inventories is included within that total
I = 19; add inventories after solving the identity
I = 7; subtract inventories twice to avoid unsold output

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9000.reason: C/D: reverse the identity and reconcile a reported investment subcomponent.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9004.q: A government purchases $18 million of new domestic flood barriers and pays $12 million in household benefits. Recipients spend $7 million on new domestic services and $3 million on imported goods, saving the rest. What GDP contribution and expenditure classification follow?

$37 million; benefits and recipient purchases both count
$28 million; imported purchases count only in C
$18 million; spending financed by benefits is excluded

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9004.reason: C/D: reconcile transfer-financed consumption and imports.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9012.q: At the start of a year, a producer has $8 million of goods made last year. It produces $30 million this year and sells $34 million, leaving $4 million in inventory. With unchanged prices, no imports and all sales to final users, which GDP account is correct?
options: $30 million: final sales 34 plus inventory investment of -4
$34 million: sales determine the production year
$38 million: add beginning inventories to new output
$42 million: add beginning inventories to final sales

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9012.reason: C/D: distinguish inventory stock, inventory change and production timing.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9017.q: A revision adds $6 billion of imported household appliances to consumption and records $2 billion of previously omitted current domestic installation services. The same imported appliances were missing from M. How should measured GDP change after all corrections?
options: Rise $2 billion; imported spending cancels while domestic installation remains
Rise $8 billion; all added consumption is domestic output
Fall $4 billion; imports are subtracted without adding their spending
Remain unchanged; every correction associated with imports cancels
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9017.feedback: C rises by 8 billion and M by 6 billion. The net 2-billion increase is the newly measured domestic service. Subtracting imports removes foreign production, not the associated domestic activity.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9017.reason: C/D: distinguish offsetting imports from additional domestic services.

PM2B1-RNGDP-H-002.q: An accountant divides current nominal GDP of $864 billion by a deflator of 120 and reports real GDP of $7.2 billion. Last year real GDP was $640 billion. Which correction and growth rate are right?
options: $720 billion real GDP; 12.5% growth
$7.2 billion real GDP; 98.9% decline
$864 billion real GDP; 35% growth
$720 billion real GDP; 20% growth
PM2B1-RNGDP-H-002.feedback: An index with base 100 requires dividing by 120/100, not 120: 864/1.2 = 720. Real growth is (720 - 640)/640 = 12.5%. The deflator’s level is not the output growth rate.
PM2B1-RNGDP-H-002.reason: B/D: replace an exam-parallel scenario with index-scaling error diagnosis and growth.

ECON-NL-ELITE-315.q: Real GDP rises 5% while nominal GDP rises 15.5%. A report calls the full nominal increase output growth. What price change and correction follow?
options: Deflator rises 10%; real production rose 5%
Deflator rises 10.5%; real production rose 15.5%
Deflator rises 20.5%; real production rose 5%
Deflator is unchanged; the two growth rates use different units

ECON-NL-ELITE-315.reason: C/D: infer the price component rather than merely assert both rose.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9005.q: A country’s nominal GDP is $468 billion and its deflator is 130. Next year real GDP rises 10%, but nominal GDP is $475.2 billion. Which new deflator and interpretation reconcile these facts?
options: 120; real output rises while the domestic price level falls
132; nominal and real growth must move together
145.2; add real growth to the old deflator
120; the lower deflator proves real production fell
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9005.feedback: Initial real GDP is 468/1.30 = 360. It grows to 396; the new deflator is 475.2/396 × 100 = 120. Output grew despite a decline in the price index from 130 to 120.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9006.q: A workshop economy makes pumps and repair visits. Base prices are $40 and $20. Current quantities are 60 pumps and an unreported number of visits; current prices are $50 and $30. Current nominal GDP is $6,000. What real GDP and deflator follow?
options: $4,400 real GDP; deflator about 136.4

$4,400 real GDP; deflator about 73.3

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9006.reason: C/D: infer missing quantity before real valuation and price-index reconstruction.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9007.q: Two new domestic goods have current prices of $12 and $30 and base prices of $10 and $20. Output of the first is 80 units; total real GDP is $2,400. A report calls $2,400 current nominal GDP. What is the correct nominal total and source of the difference?
options: $3,360; recover 80 units of the second good and value both at current prices

$4,320; current prices must be applied to the dollar value of real GDP

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9007.reason: C/D: missing quantity and current-price reconstruction.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9013.q: Nominal GDP grows 8% and the GDP deflator grows 12.5%. Population is unchanged. Which conclusion best evaluates the claim that average real production rose?
options: Real GDP per person falls 4%; nominal growth does not establish output growth

Real GDP per person rises 8%; population did not change

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9013.reason: C/D: opposite nominal/real movement with exact index interpretation.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9022.q: Nominal GDP rises 32% over two years. Real GDP rises 10% in the first year and is unchanged in the second. The deflator started at 125. Which final deflator and cumulative price change follow?

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9022.reason: C/D: multi-period output/price reconstruction and base-versus-period distinction.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9014.q: Two regions report real GDP per person of $44,000 and $40,000. In the first, output per hour is $40 and annual hours per resident are 1,100; in the second they are $50 and 800. Which comparison is supported without assigning a value to leisure?

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9014.reason: C/D: integrate output, hours and a disciplined welfare inference.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9015.q: After a storm, rebuilding adds $12 million of current production while lost business activity reduces other current production by $5 million. Destroyed existing buildings were worth $30 million. Which GDP and welfare statement is defensible?

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9015.reason: C/D: distinguish a flow change, lost wealth and welfare rather than repeat a disaster slogan.

ECON-NL-ELITE-321.q: A basket costs $750 when the CPI is 125. One year later the same basket costs $810. Which new index and claim about inflation are correct?

CPI 162; inflation is 35%, measured from the base year

ECON-NL-ELITE-321.reason: C/D: reverse the basket base and connect the new index to inflation.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9023.q: A fixed basket contains 3 tickets and 2 repairs. Base prices are $8 and $18. Last year the basket cost $72. This year its CPI is 135 and each ticket costs $9. What repair price and annual inflation rate are implied?

$40.50 per repair and 35% inflation

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9023.reason: C/D: reconstruct a missing price and chain the basket index to annual inflation.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9024.q: An index is rebased: the old series lists last year at 160 and this year at 176, while the new series sets last year to 100. A nominal benefit rose 6% over the period. Which comparison survives rebasing?

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9024.reason: C/D: distinguish index rebasing from inflation and evaluate a real payment.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9025.q: A basket contains 4 units of A at a base price of $6 and an unknown quantity of B at $12. Its base cost is $72. Current prices are $9 for A and $15 for B. Which CPI and next-period inflation follow if the same basket then costs $100.80?

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9025.reason: C/D: infer basket quantity before index and inflation calculations.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9026.q: A nominal hourly wage rises from $25 to $27. Basket cost rises from $500 to $540, then falls to $525 while the wage stays $27. Relative to the starting year, what real-wage change remains after both price movements?

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9026.reason: C/D: multi-period real-wage interpretation with an intervening price reversal.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9027.q: A fixed basket’s cost rises 20% in one year and falls 10% in the next. A commentator claims prices are back where they started because growth has reversed. Which cumulative index and purchasing-power statement are correct, starting from 100?

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9027.reason: C/D: compound inflation and evaluate a misleading reversal claim.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9028.q: A basket agency sees households replacing a newly expensive rail route with an existing bus route. A trial finds the cheaper travel bundle preserves the same commuting service. Which evidence supports substitution bias, and what does it fail to establish?
options: A fixed bundle overstates the cost of that service; the evidence does not quantify bias for the whole CPI

The change proves the whole CPI should fall because one alternative is cheaper

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9028.reason: C: evaluate equivalence evidence and inference limits rather than identify a label.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9029.q: A new pump costs 12% more than the old model and lasts 12% longer with identical annual performance and maintenance costs. Ignoring discounting, which conclusion is supported for this product, and which is not?

Economy-wide inflation is zero because this product has no service-cost rise

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9029.reason: C/D: quantify a controlled quality comparison and limit its interpretation.

PM2B2-BIAS-L-001.q: A fixed basket costs 9% more, while a redesigned bundle costs only 3% more. Before concluding that substitution bias is six percentage points, what must an analyst establish?
options: The redesigned bundle preserves the relevant living standard, with comparable quality and coverage
Households bought fewer total items, regardless of the services they lost
Both bundles contain the same number of product names, regardless of quantities
The redesigned bundle is cheaper, even if it provides less value

PM2B2-BIAS-L-001.reason: C: evaluate the missing identifying condition in a plausible bias calculation.

PM2B2-DEF-H-002.q: Between two years, individual prices do not change, but domestic production shifts toward goods whose current prices are higher relative to their base-year prices. Why can a fixed-base GDP deflator rise?
options: Current quantities put more weight on goods with larger price increases since the base year

The deflator begins including imported consumer goods as domestic output
A shift toward goods with higher dollar prices raises every index regardless of base prices

PM2B2-DEF-H-002.reason: B: clarify the ambiguous meaning of relative prices; preserve composition skill.

ECON-NL-ELITE-331.q: A government must update a household allowance and also convert nominal GDP to real GDP. Imported household energy gets dearer while domestic investment equipment gets cheaper. Which pairing and interpretation fit?
options: Use CPI for the allowance and the GDP deflator for GDP; the indexes can move differently
Use the GDP deflator for both because energy purchases reduce net exports
Use CPI for both because every domestic output price is in its basket
Use either index for either task because all price changes have equal weights

ECON-NL-ELITE-331.reason: C: apply index choice to competing household and production tasks.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9032.q: An economy’s consumer basket has base spending of $40 on imported tea and $60 on domestic services. Tea prices rise 25%; services prices stay fixed. The only other domestic output is exported machinery, whose price falls 10%. With quantities fixed, which conclusion is justified?
options: CPI rises 10%; the GDP deflator falls, but its size needs domestic-output weights
Both indexes rise 25% because imports are in consumer spending
CPI rises 25%; the GDP deflator falls exactly 10%
CPI is unchanged; imported consumer prices are excluded

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9032.reason: C/D: calculate one index while recognizing information insufficient for another.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9033.q: Domestic output consists of 10 machines and 100 services. Base prices are $100 and $10; current prices are $120 and $10. Consumers buy the services and imported clothing; the clothing price is unchanged. Which price-index account is supported?
options: GDP deflator 110; CPI unchanged if its fixed basket contains only those consumer purchases
GDP deflator 120; CPI rises 20% because domestic machines got dearer
GDP deflator 110; CPI must rise by the same 10%
GDP deflator 100; business equipment is not final domestic output

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9033.reason: C/D: quantify domestic-output weighting and distinguish consumer coverage.

PM2B2-DEF-L-002.q: A household grant rises from $2,000 to $2,160 as CPI moves from 125 to 135. Nominal GDP rises 8% while the GDP deflator rises 4%. Which combined assessment uses the appropriate indexes?
options: The grant preserves purchasing power; real GDP rises about 3.8%
The grant gains 8% purchasing power; real GDP rises 8%
The grant loses purchasing power; real GDP is unchanged
Both real changes are zero because each nominal value rose 8%

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9080.q: Spending and total vacancies recover after a downturn, but vacancies concentrate in licensed occupations while displaced workers lack the credentials. Which evidence would most directly strengthen a structural diagnosis over a purely cyclical one?
options: Credential training is followed by placements into the unfilled occupations while overall spending changes little
All vacancies disappear when spending weakens again
Workers have suitable offers and are briefly choosing among them
Unemployment falls only when economy-wide spending rises sharply, with no change in skills
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9080.feedback: The mismatch between expanding occupations and worker credentials points to a structural barrier. Placements after relevant training, with demand broadly unchanged, strengthen that mechanism rather than a claim based only on weak spending or ordinary search.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9080.reason: C: choose discriminating evidence among plausible unemployment mechanisms.

PM2B4-UTYPE-L-002.q: A city’s jobless population includes skilled movers choosing among local openings and workers whose occupation disappeared. A single faster job-listing service is proposed for both. Which prediction is best supported?
options: It can shorten matching for the first group; the second may also need retraining or mobility support
It must eliminate both groups’ unemployment because each can read the same vacancies
It affects only cyclical unemployment because information is part of total spending
It turns structurally unemployed workers into employed people as soon as listings are viewed
PM2B4-UTYPE-L-002.feedback: The first group faces search frictions among suitable jobs. The second faces a durable mismatch that information alone may not remove. Diagnosis should guide the intervention without assuming guaranteed placement.
PM2B4-UTYPE-L-002.reason: C: distinguish unemployment mechanisms through a conditional remedy.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9076.q: In a competitive labor market, employment is 100 at the clearing wage. A binding wage floor produces labor supply of 140 and demand of 95. Assuming everyone seeking work is available and active, which comparison is correct?
options: Employment falls by 5, while the labor surplus is 45; these are different quantities
Employment falls by 45 because every person in the surplus previously had a job
Employment falls by 40, matching the increase in labor supply
There is no surplus because 95 people remain employed
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9076.feedback: Employment changes from 100 to 95, a loss of 5. The new excess of labor supplied over labor demanded is 140 - 95 = 45, including the effect of increased job seeking as well as reduced hiring. The surplus is not the number of pre-existing jobs lost.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9076.reason: B/C/D: distinguish a wage-floor labor surplus from employment loss.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9077.q: A benefit extension lowers the cost of continued search. A simultaneous placement program improves matching. Average unemployment duration then falls. Which conclusion is warranted from these facts alone?
options: The combined outcome improved duration; it does not show that the benefit extension by itself shortened search
The fall proves benefit extensions always shorten search
The extension must have been ineffective at protecting income because duration fell
The placement program cannot matter because benefits determine every search decision
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9077.feedback: Income support can reduce search urgency while better matching shortens search. Their combined result does not isolate either effect; a credible separate comparison would be needed. The duration result also does not measure the value of income protection.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9077.reason: C: evaluate competing institutional channels and causal limits.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9078.q: A negotiated wage rises from $20 to $24 while employment falls from 100 to 90, with hours per worker fixed. What happens to the total wage bill, and what distributional claim is justified?
options: The wage bill rises 8%; retained workers gain hourly pay while some workers lose jobs
The wage bill falls 10%; no workers gain from the contract
The wage bill rises 20%; the employment change is irrelevant
The wage bill rises 8%; this proves every original worker is better off
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9078.feedback: The wage bill changes from 20 × 100 = 2,000 to 24 × 90 = 2,160 per common unit of hours, an 8% rise. The aggregate increase does not erase the job losses; gains to retained workers and losses to displaced workers differ.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9078.reason: C/D: integrate a union wage/employment account and insider-outsider interpretation.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9079.q: A firm considers raising wages from $18 to $21 per hour. Output per hour is expected to rise from 6 to 7 units through better retention and effort, with other unit costs unchanged. Which cost calculation and caution are correct?
options: Wage cost stays $3 per unit if the productivity forecast holds; the forecast still needs evidence
$3.50 per unit is certain because productivity cannot respond to wages
$2.57 per unit is certain because the old wage applies to the new output
$3 per unit proves the wage policy eliminates unemployment throughout the economy
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9079.feedback: The old wage cost is 18/6 = 3 per unit; the proposed cost is 21/7 = 3 if the effort/retention forecast occurs. This makes an efficiency-wage rationale possible, but does not prove the forecast or settle economy-wide unemployment.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9079.reason: C/D: test an efficiency-wage calculation with a conditional rather than guaranteed conclusion.

ECON-NL-ELITE-375.q: A wage floor is $16. At that wage, 112 workers seek jobs and firms hire 88. A demand increase raises desired hiring to 100 while the wage and labor supply stay fixed. What happens to the labor surplus?
options: It falls from 24 to 12; higher labor demand reduces the excess supply
It stays at 24 because the statutory wage did not change
It rises from 24 to 36 because firms want more labor
It disappears because any increase in demand makes a floor nonbinding
ECON-NL-ELITE-375.feedback: Initially the surplus is 112 - 88 = 24. With hiring demand of 100, it is 112 - 100 = 12. The wage floor can remain binding even as the size of the labor surplus changes.
ECON-NL-ELITE-375.reason: C/D: compare labor-market outcomes under an unchanged institution.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9075.q: An economy has 2% frictional, 3% structural and 2% cyclical unemployment. A recovery eliminates the cyclical component. At the same time, better matching lowers frictional unemployment to 1.5%, with structural unemployment unchanged. What actual and natural rates remain?
options: Both are 4.5%; recovery removed the cyclical component and matching lowered the natural rate
Both are 5%; recovery cannot change any observed unemployment rate
Actual is 2.5% and natural is 4.5%; subtract the cyclical decline again
Both are zero because the recession has ended
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9075.feedback: After recovery, cyclical unemployment is zero. The remaining natural rate is 1.5 + 3 = 4.5%, also the actual rate. Ending the downturn and improving normal matching are distinct channels.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9075.reason: C/D: decompose a changing natural rate and a disappearing cyclical gap.

ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9085.q: Actual unemployment falls from 9% to 7%. Over the same interval, an estimate of the natural rate falls from 6% to 4%. What happens to the cyclical gap, and what claim would overstate the evidence?
options: The gap stays at 3 points; the lower actual rate alone does not show cyclical weakness diminished
The gap falls 2 points; actual unemployment determines the gap by itself
The gap rises 2 points; a lower natural rate always raises the gap by that amount
The gap becomes zero because both rates fell equally
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9085.feedback: Initially the gap is 9 - 6 = 3 points; finally it is 7 - 4 = 3. Actual unemployment fell with the estimated natural benchmark, so these numbers do not show a smaller cyclical component.
ECON-NL-LEGENDARY-9085.reason: C/D: compare moving actual and natural rates rather than one subtraction.

PM2B4-NRU-L-002.q: A retraining reform is expected to lower structural unemployment by 1 percentage point, but longer voluntary search raises frictional unemployment by 0.4 point. Cyclical unemployment is unchanged. Which natural-rate prediction follows, conditional on both estimates?
options: It falls 0.6 point; the policy effects partly offset
It falls 1.4 points; both changes reduce unemployment
It rises 0.4 point; structural mismatch is outside the natural rate
It stays unchanged; only recessions can move the natural rate
PM2B4-NRU-L-002.feedback: The natural rate includes both structural and frictional unemployment. Its predicted change is -1 + 0.4 = -0.6 percentage point. The net estimate is conditional on the two stated mechanisms, not a guarantee about every retraining policy.
PM2B4-NRU-L-002.reason: C/D: conditional natural-rate recommendation with competing components.

ECON-NL-ELITE-379.q: Two economies each have 5% natural unemployment. One combines 1% frictional and 4% structural unemployment; the other combines 3% frictional and 2% structural. Which policy comparison fits these equal totals?
options: The first has more mismatch to address; the second has more scope for faster matching, holding effectiveness comparable
The same natural rate proves their underlying labor-market problems are identical
Only the second has natural unemployment because frictional unemployment is the sole component
Both can reach zero unemployment simply by ending a recession
ECON-NL-ELITE-379.feedback: Both totals equal 5%, but the components differ. A common aggregate benchmark does not establish identical barriers or identical policy priorities. Relevant retraining and matching interventions target different components.
ECON-NL-ELITE-379.reason: C: infer differing policy needs from the same natural-rate total.
